summary: The note traces the history of the Estonian language, from its becoming the state language after the Estonian War of Independence in 1919 to its spread among non-Estonian residents. It notes that Estonians were 97.3% of the population and spoke the language in 1945, and that the share of ethnic Estonians rose back above 70% after Soviet immigrants returned to their countries of origin. It also describes the two historical Estonian languages, North and South Estonian, which derive from two migration waves, and states that modern standard Estonian is based on Northern Estonian dialects.
one_line: Overview of the Estonian language's history, from its status as state language after 1919 to its dialect origins and spread among non-Estonian residents.
key_facts: After the Estonian War of Independence in 1919, the Estonian language became the state language of the newly independent country.
In 1945, 97.3% of Estonia considered itself ethnic Estonian and spoke the language.
The return of Soviet immigrants to their countries of origin brought the proportion of Estonians in Estonia back above 70%.
About 40% of the remaining non-Estonians in Estonia had adopted the Estonian language at the 2000 census.
The note states that many remnant non-Estonians in Estonia have adopted the Estonian language, as in Latvia.
The two historical Estonian languages, North Estonian and South Estonian, are sometimes considered dialects.
North and South Estonian are based on the ancestors of modern Estonians' migration into the territory of Estonia in at least two different waves.
Both North and South Estonian groups spoke considerably different Finnic vernaculars.
Modern standard Estonian has evolved on the basis of the dialects of Northern Estonia.
